query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Under high‐temperature wear conditions (800–900 °C), the overall wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is predominantly governed by the rapid formation of a continuous, adherent mixed oxide layer that protects the underlying metal from severe abrasive and adhesive wear.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, nanocrystalline FeNiCrCoCu thin protective coating applied on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Pre-oxidize a set of coatings by heating them in air (e.g., at 800 °C for a predetermined duration) to induce controlled oxide scale formation, then compare their high-temperature wear behavior with that of as-deposited (non-pre-oxidized) coatings.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear tests conducted in air at 800–900 °C under representative loading conditions (e.g., reciprocating wear test with ~26 N applied force for 900 s) to simulate service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, mixed oxide film (composed of oxides from Fe, Ni, Co, and Cr—with possible contributions from Cu oxides or Cu segregation effects) that forms on the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, selective oxidation of the elements in the FeNiCrCoCu alloy leads to the in-situ formation of a protective oxide layer. This oxide film acts as a barrier, reducing direct metal-to-metal contact, lowering friction, and thereby mitigating severe abrasive or adhesive wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings that are pre-oxidized to develop a robust oxide scale should exhibit significantly lower wear depths and reduced coefficients of friction compared to unmodified, as-deposited coatings under identical high-temperature wear testing.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without any pre-oxidation treatment, subjected to high-temperature wear.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under oxidizing atmospheres at temperatures of 800–900 °C and under wear loading conditions typical of high-temperature applications; behavior at lower temperatures or in inert atmospheres may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The precise composition, phase stability, and mechanical properties of the oxide scale are not fully known due to potential segregation effects (e.g., from Cu) and limited prior studies on this specific alloy system in high-temperature wear regimes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two identical sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings on a conventional metal substrate. Pre-oxidize one set in air at 800 °C for a fixed time to develop a continuous oxide layer, while leaving the other set as-deposited. Subject both sets to reciprocating wear tests in air at 800–900 °C under a load of approximately 26 N for 900 s. Characterize the worn surfaces using SEM and XRD to assess the oxide film continuity and measure wear depth and coefficient of friction.
measurements: Surface oxide composition and thickness (via SEM/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in wear depth and lower COF compared to the as-deposited coatings, or if no continuous protective oxide film is observed on the pre-oxidized samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Findings: The as-deposited film exhibited a nanocrystalline body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm and a thickness of ~900 nm.; Nanoindentation measurement
